config.title: Hotel or Apartment in Berlin - FAQ
config.subtitle: How the three accommodation types are priced in Berlin, the registration number every holiday flat must show, and which one fits which trip.

items.q: Is a hotel or an apartment better in Berlin?
items.a: **It depends on your party size and how long you are staying, because the two are priced in different shapes.** A hotel charges per room and a room sleeps two, so a party of three needs a second room. An apartment charges one price for the whole flat whatever the party size, but adds a cleaning fee that is charged once. That makes hotels competitive for one or two people on short stays, and apartments competitive from roughly three travellers or four nights upwards. Berlin adds a 7.5 % accommodation tax to both.

items.q: What is the registration number on a Berlin apartment listing?
items.a: **It is the permit number Berlin issues to legal holiday rentals, and it has to be publicly visible in the listing.** Under the Zweckentfremdungsverbot, anyone advertising a whole flat to visitors has had to display it since 1 August 2018. The Berlin Senate describes it as a mix of digits, letters and special characters, 17 characters in total. If you cannot find one in a whole-flat listing, ask the host for it in writing before you pay.

items.q: What happens if a Berlin apartment has no registration number?
items.a: **The host risks the fine and you risk the cancellation.** Berlin fines unpermitted holiday letting heavily, and the Mitte district office states penalties of up to 500,000 euros. You are not the one penalised, but since EU Regulation 2024/1028 started applying on 20 May 2026, platforms have to verify registration numbers and report host data to a national digital entry point. An unregistered Berlin listing is now much more likely to be delisted between the day you book and the day you arrive, which leaves you looking for a room at short notice.

items.q: Does Berlin city tax apply to apartments and hostels too?
items.a: **Yes, all of them.** The Berlin accommodation tax is 7.5 % of the net accommodation price and covers hotels, hostels, guesthouses, holiday flats, holiday houses and rooms in private homes. Breakfast, the minibar, parking and similar extras sit outside the taxed amount. Business travel lost its exemption on 1 April 2024, and from 1 January 2026 the old ten-bed threshold that kept the smallest operators out of the tax was removed.

items.q: Are hostels in Berlin only for young travellers?
items.a: **No, and most Berlin hostels sell private rooms as well as dorm beds.** The thing to watch is where the price sits. A private twin room in a Berlin hostel is usually priced closer to a budget hotel than to a bunk, so compare it against hotel rooms rather than against dorm prices. Dorm beds are priced per person per night, which means they are the only one of the three options that gets more expensive with both extra travellers and extra nights.

items.q: How much does the cleaning fee matter on a Berlin apartment?
items.a: **A lot on a short stay and almost nothing on a long one, because it is charged once.** On a two-night weekend a typical cleaning fee can be a fifth of the total and it is the single thing most likely to make an apartment lose to a hotel. Spread across eight or ten nights it disappears into the nightly rate. Work out the number of nights at which the flat overtakes the rooms before you start browsing listings.

items.q: Where should I stay in Berlin for a walking tour of the centre?
items.a: **Anywhere with a direct connection to Alexanderplatz.** The historic centre is compact and the free BerlinWalk tour starts at the World Clock on Alexanderplatz, running about two hours through 11 stops and 16 places before finishing at Hackescher Markt. Mitte, Prenzlauer Berg, Friedrichshain and the northern edge of Kreuzberg all reach it easily. Before booking accommodation, put the address into a map and check the travel time to Alexanderplatz. That number tells you more about how your days will feel than the listing photos do.
